prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Kalah on a standard board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(you: list[int], opponent: list[int]) -> int: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - The game uses 6 houses per side plus 1 store per side. - The state is given as two lists of length 7: - `you = [h0, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, store]` - `opponent = [h0, h1, h2, h3, h4, h5, store]` - Indices `0..5` are houses; index `6` is that player's store. - All entries are non-negative integers (seed counts). - Game ends when one player has no seeds in all houses (`0..5` all zero). - When the game ends, the other player moves all remaining seeds into their store; higher store total wins (draws possible). - You may assume `policy` is never called when you have no legal move. # Action / Return Format - Choose an integer move `i` where `0 <= i <= 5` and `you[i] > 0`. - Sow by removing all seeds from `you[i]` and placing them one-by-one in order: - `you[i+1]` through `you[5]`, then `you[6]` (your store), then `opponent[0]` through `opponent[5]`, then `you[0]` through `you[5]`, repeating as needed. - Skip `opponent[6]` (the opponent's store) when sowing. - Extra move: if the last seed lands in `you[6]`, you immediately get another move. - Capture: if the last seed lands in your house `you[i]` (`0..5`) and that house was empty before the drop, and the opposite house `opponent[5 - i]` has seeds, capture the seed in `you[i]` and all seeds in `opponent[5 - i]` into `you[6]`. - You must always return a legal move integer `i` with `you[i] > 0`. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm building a Kalah game engine with minimax and alpha-beta pruning, representing the board state as my side and opponent side with 7 positions each, then implementing a move simulator that handles sowing, extra turns, and captures.

Writing the game simulator...

I'll check for game end conditions when all houses on either side are empty, then set up minimax to maximize my store score. Building the policy function... Implementing the game logic and search algorithm... I'm finishing up the iterative deepening loop—updating the best move when a better one is found at each depth, catching timeouts, and checking if we've exceeded the deadline before incrementing depth. Then I'm verifying the apply_move logic with some test cases: the standard opening move from house 0 distributes seeds correctly without capturing, moving from house 2 lands in the store for an extra turn, and I'm checking the capture mechanics work as expected.

For optimization, I'm considering move ordering to prioritize moves that grant extra turns since they tend to be stronger and help alpha-beta pruning, though I'm keeping it simple with iterative deepening for now. I'm estimating depth 10-12 should be reachable given the branching factor and pruning effectiveness. I'll skip the transposition table for now and just ensure we always return a legal move as a fallback.

On evaluation, I'm noticing a potential inconsistency between terminal and non-terminal positions—terminal evaluation uses total seeds while heuristic evaluation uses store difference. I'm resolving this by using store difference consistently for both, since the final evaluation just represents what the stores would be if all remaining seeds were collected. This keeps the values comparable and the heuristic naturally underestimates since seeds can still move into stores.

Implementing the move application logic... I'm verifying the turn logic for the minimax search—when I get an extra turn, I stay in control, but when my opponent gets one, they keep their turn. Now I'm implementing the policy function that will search for the best move within the time constraint.

I'm using iterative deepening to progressively search deeper, evaluating each candidate move and tracking the best one found so far. If I run out of time mid-iteration, I fall back to the best move from the previous completed depth. The alpha-beta pruning should help cut down the search space significantly, and using the final evaluation directly for terminal positions ensures accuracy at the end of the game.
